title: Next: The Copper Lattice
summary: Closing splash turns one successful water-access proof into a scale problem: requests are multiplying faster than one rocket and one relay can answer them.
panelPlan: Full-page closing splash with no conventional panel grid. Use the Launch-Shop work wall and bench after sunrise: one completed authorization card is surrounded by a fast-growing scatter of new community requests, while a small orbital-track sketch or fading relay icon shows the narrowness of the existing solution.
Keep the crew peripheral or silhouetted at work rather than posed. The visual subject is the multiplication of requests around one tiny proof of concept.
Do not show ground relays, a lattice, legacy timing modules or any specific Issue 2 solution. The page should make the next engineering problem feel inevitable without answering it.
Integrate the captions as bold closing-page typography that accelerates toward the final NEXT line.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Esperanza has three days of water.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: By sunrise, seven communities have asked for help.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: That is the trouble with proving something can be done.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: People start asking you to do it again.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: A rocket can win a few minutes.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: If this is going to become more than one impossible night, the next thing they build has to survive without depending on one rocket, one satellite or one person.

directionInline.text: This is a non-diegetic closing teaser. Preserve exact caption text. Re-arm only what the reader now knows: one proof worked, requests are multiplying, and the current solution cannot scale. Do not depict or name the ground-relay solution, clock synchronization, alternate routing, seized nodes or any later Issue 2 event.
